claim: Arabidopsis accessions Cape Verde Islands-0 (Cvi) and C24 produce seeds with high and low dormancy levels, respectively, when cultivated under standard laboratory conditions.
source: When cultivated under standard laboratory conditions, Arabidopsis accessions Cape Verde Islands-0 (Cvi) and C24 (C24) produce seeds with high and low dormancy levels, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with supporting germination data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cvi seeds require a longer dry after-ripening time than C24 seeds to acquire the capacity to germinate.
source: Cvi seeds require a longer dry after-ripening time than C24 seeds to acquire the capacity to germinate.
evidence: Directly stated and supported by germination data in Figure 1A showing differential germination rates at different after-ripening periods.

claim: Following a short after-ripening period (five days), C24, Cvi, and F1 seeds were unable to germinate 72 hr after seed imbibition.
source: Following a short after-ripening period (five days), C24, Cvi, and F1 seeds were unable to germinate 72 hr after seed imbibition (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A long dry after-ripening period (6 months) led to full germination of all seed groups (C24, Cvi, and F1 seeds).
source: As expected, a long dry after-ripening period (6 months) led to full germination of all seed groups (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 1A.

claim: An intermediate after-ripening time (25 days) led to full germination of C24 seeds but not of Cvi seeds.
source: An intermediate after-ripening time (25 days) led to full germination of C24 seeds but not of Cvi seeds, consistent with their different natural seed dormancy levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 1A.

claim: C24xCvi F1 seeds almost fully germinated after intermediate after-ripening (25 days), unlike CvixC24 F1 seeds.
source: Interestingly, C24xCvi F1 seeds almost fully germinated, unlike CvixC24 F1 seeds, indicating that C24xCvi F1 seeds are less dormant than CvixC24 F1 seeds (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 1A.

claim: C24xCvi F1 seeds are less dormant than CvixC24 F1 seeds.
source: Interestingly, C24xCvi F1 seeds almost fully germinated, unlike CvixC24 F1 seeds, indicating that C24xCvi F1 seeds are less dormant than CvixC24 F1 seeds (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 1A.

claim: Removal of the testa and endosperm triggered embryonic growth in dormant seeds.
source: In all cases where seeds were dormant, removal of the testa and endosperm triggered embryonic growth, consistent with previous results (Figure 1A) (Bethke et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated in text, supported by images in Figure 1A, and referenced to previous studies.

claim: Hybrid F1 seeds produced by Cvi and C24 reciprocal crosses tend to inherit dormancy levels more akin to those of the maternal ecotype.
source: Here we showed that hybrid seeds produced by Cvi and C24 reciprocal crosses or Cvi and Col reciprocal crosses tend to inherit dormancy levels more akin to those of the maternal ecotype (Figure 1).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 1.

claim: Hybrid F1 seeds produced by Cvi and Col reciprocal crosses tend to inherit dormancy levels more akin to those of the maternal ecotype.
source: Here we showed that hybrid seeds produced by Cvi and C24 reciprocal crosses or Cvi and Col reciprocal crosses tend to inherit dormancy levels more akin to those of the maternal ecotype (Figure 1).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 1C.

claim: The endosperm's germination-repressive activity is essential to implement maternally imposed and cold-induced dormancy levels.
source: We also showed that the endosperm's germination-repressive activity is essential to implement maternally imposed and cold-induced dormancy levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: CvixC24tet F1 seeds were more dormant than C24xCvitet F1 seeds.
source: Furthermore, CvixC24tet F1 seeds were more dormant than C24xCvitet F1 seeds (Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 1B.

claim: The endosperm's natural maternal genome imbalance does not readily account for the observed inheritance in F1 seeds of dormancy levels akin to those of their maternal genotype.
source: These data therefore indicate that the endosperm's natural maternal genome imbalance does not readily account for the observed inheritance in F1 seeds of dormancy levels akin to those of their maternal genotype (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of tetraploid crosses shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mature testa does not contain obvious traces of organelles, cytoplasm or nuclei according to electron microscopy studies.
source: Electron microscopy studies reveal that the mature testa does not contain obvious traces of organelles, cytoplasm or nuclei (Yadav et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Yadav et al., 2014.

claim: The concentration levels of RNA extracted from testas were below detection levels, unlike those from partially and fully dissected endosperm.
source: The concentration levels of RNA extracted from testas were below detection levels, unlike those from partially and fully dissected endosperm (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The total number of reads obtained with the testa sample was only about 1% of the read numbers obtained for the partially and fully dissected endosperm.
source: The total number of reads obtained with the testa sample was only about 1% of the read numbers obtained for the partially and fully dissected endosperm (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by sequencing data in Table 1.

claim: Only 14 genes among 33,557 annotated genes were differentially expressed between the partially and fully dissected endosperm samples (p < 0.05).
source: Only 14 genes among 33,557 annotated genes were differentially expressed between the partially and fully dissected endosperm samples (p < 0.05) (Figure 2—source data 1) (Material and methods).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Among the 14 differentially expressed genes between partially and fully dissected endosperm, seven are osmotic stress-induced genes whose expression was higher in the fully dissected endosperm.
source: Among these 14 genes, seven are osmotic stress-induced genes whose expression was higher in the fully dissected endosperm relative to the partially dissected endosperm (Figure 2—source data 2) (Kilian et al., 2007; Winter et al., 2007).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2—source data 2 and citations.

claim: Low amounts of mRNA are present in the testa relative to the endosperm.
source: Altogether, these results confirm the notion that low amounts of mRNA are present in the testa relative to the endosperm and that the partially dissected endosperm of mature seeds can be used as a source of endospermic mRNA without a major concern of maternal mRNA contamination (see also below).
evidence: Directly stated in text based on RNA extraction and sequencing data presented in Table 1 and related analyses.

claim: The partially dissected endosperm of mature seeds can be used as a source of endospermic mRNA without a major concern of maternal mRNA contamination.
source: Altogether, these results confirm the notion that low amounts of mRNA are present in the testa relative to the endosperm and that the partially dissected endosperm of mature seeds can be used as a source of endospermic mRNA without a major concern of maternal mRNA contamination (see also below).
evidence: Directly stated in text based on RNA extraction and sequencing data.

claim: 71 maternally expressed genes (MEGs) and 5 paternally expressed genes (PEGs) were identified in the endosperm from dormant CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds.
source: In the endosperm from dormant CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds, we identified 71 maternally expressed genes (MEGs) and 5 paternally expressed genes (PEGs) (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 3.

claim: 50 MEGs and 8 PEGs were identified in the endosperm from non-dormant CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds.
source: In the endosperm from non-dormant CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds, we identified 50 MEGs and 8 PEGs (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 3.

claim: Only 14 MEGs and 2 PEGs were present in both dormant and non-dormant data sets.
source: Only 14 MEGs and 2 PEGs were present in both dormant and non-dormant data sets (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by Venn diagram in Figure 2B.

claim: Among the 107 MEGs, only two (AT4G00220 and AT4G04955) had at least one read in the testa cDNA library.
source: Among the 107 MEGs, only two (AT4G00220 and AT4G04955) had at least one read (Table 2).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: The total read number of AT4G00220 and AT4G04955 in the testa was less than 1-2% of that found in the partially or fully dissected endosperm cDNA libraries.
source: However, their total read number was less than 1-2% of that found in the partially or fully dissected endosperm cDNA libraries (Table 2).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: None of the MEGs had expression levels that were significantly different between partially and fully dissected endosperm samples.
source: Furthermore, as indicated above, none of the MEGs had expression levels that were significantly different between partially and fully dissected endosperm samples (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2—source data 2.

claim: RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing on 17 MEGs and 2 PEGs in independent CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 endosperm material confirmed the RNA-seq analysis.
source: To validate the occurrence of imprinting, we performed RT-PCR on 17 MEGs and 2 PEGs in independent CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 endosperm material. Amplicons were sequenced by Sanger and MiSeq sequencing (see Materials and methods). The results confirmed the RNA-seq analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by sequencing data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—source data 2.

claim: Analysis of F1 transgenic seed material confirmed the maternal expression of the pFWA::dFWA-GFP transgene in mature endosperm.
source: Analysis of the F1 transgenic seed material confirmed the maternal expression of the pFWA::dFWA-GFP transgene in mature endosperm (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by confocal microscopy and RT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Only 6 MEGs and 3 PEGs found in mature endosperm were previously reported during early embryogenesis, including the MEG FWA.
source: We compared the identified endospermic MEGs and PEGs with those reported during early embryogenesis using the same F1 seed material (Pignatta et al., 2014). Only 6 MEGs and 3 PEGs found here were previously reported, including the MEG FWA (Figure 2B) (Pignatta et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by Venn diagram in Figure 2B and citation to Pignatta et al., 2014.

claim: Specific programs of endospermic genomic imprinting take place upon seed imbibition.
source: These results strongly suggest the occurrence of specific programs of endospermic genomic imprinting that take place upon seed imbibition.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on identification of different sets of imprinted genes in dormant vs non-dormant seeds.

claim: Imprinted gene expression programs appear to change according to seed dormancy levels.
source: Furthermore, these imprinted gene expression programs appear to change according to seed dormancy levels.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on identification of dormancy-specific and non-dormant-specific imprinted genes.

claim: Among the 57 dormancy-specific MEGs, seven were shown to regulate dormancy or germination.
source: Indeed, among the 57 dormancy-specific MEGs, seven were shown to regulate dormancy or germination, whereas another nine could potentially perform the same role based on current knowledge (Supplementary file 1 and see below).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Among the 57 dormancy-specific MEGs, another nine could potentially regulate dormancy or germination based on current knowledge.
source: Indeed, among the 57 dormancy-specific MEGs, seven were shown to regulate dormancy or germination, whereas another nine could potentially perform the same role based on current knowledge (Supplementary file 1 and see below).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Only three genes that directly (two genes) or indirectly (one gene) regulate germination were among the 36 non-dormant-specific MEGs.
source: By contrast, only three genes that directly (two genes) or indirectly (one gene) regulate germination were among the 36 non-dormant-specific MEGs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: About half (26 out of 57) of the dormancy-specific MEGs had expression levels that were negatively correlated with seed dormancy levels.
source: Clustering analysis of gene expression levels revealed that among the 57 identified dormancy-specific MEGs, about half (26 out of 57) had expression levels that were negatively correlated with seed dormancy levels: Cvi seeds being the most dormant, followed by CvixCol F1, ColxCvi F1 and finally Col seeds, which are the least dormant (cluster 1 in Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by clustering analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: The majority of MEGs (12 out of 16) that are involved or potentially involved in regulating seed germination belonged to cluster 1.
source: Strikingly, the majority of MEGs (12 out of 16) that are involved or potentially involved in regulating seed germination belonged to cluster 1 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 2D.

claim: Among all Arabidopsis genes only a minority (about 7%) had expression levels that negatively correlated with seed dormancy levels.
source: Furthermore, among all Arabidopsis genes only a minority (about 7%) had expression levels that negatively correlated with seed dormancy levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Genes belonging to the dormancy-specific MEG group tend to have expression levels that correlate negatively with seed dormancy levels.
source: These data therefore indicate that genes belonging to the dormancy-specific MEG group tend to have expression levels that correlate negatively with seed dormancy levels.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on clustering analysis and comparison with genome-wide expression patterns.

claim: Cultivating Arabidopsis plants under low temperatures (10°C) increases final seed dormancy levels.
source: Cultivating Arabidopsis plants under low temperatures (10°C) increases final seed dormancy levels (Figure 2E).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: The presence of an intact endosperm is necessary to repress the germination of highly dormant seeds produced under low temperatures.
source: Using seed nicking experiments, a previous report indicated that the presence of an intact endosperm is necessary to repress the germination of highly dormant seeds produced under low temperatures (Kendall et al., 2011). Indeed, we observed that removal of the endosperm and testa, but not removal of the testa alone, triggered embryonic growth and greening (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Directly stated in text, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6, and cited to Kendall et al., 2011.

claim: The endosperm is necessary to repress the germination of highly dormant seeds that developed under low temperatures.
source: This demonstrates that the endosperm is also necessary to repress the germination of highly dormant seeds that developed under low temperatures.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on seed dissection experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Among the 57 dormant-specific MEGs, about half (33) had their expression lowered when seeds developed under cold temperatures.
source: Strikingly, among the 57 dormant-specific MEGs, about half (33) had their expression lowered when seeds developed under cold temperatures (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2E and Figure 2—source data 5.

claim: Among the 36 MEGs identified in non-dormant seeds, only one had its expression lowered by cold while the expression of the vast majority of genes was unchanged.
source: By contrast, among the 36 MEGs identified in non-dormant seeds, only one had its expression lowered while the expression of the vast majority of genes was unchanged.
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: The majority (23 out of 33) of the genes that were downregulated in response to cold belonged to the cluster 1 of genes whose expression negatively correlates with dormancy levels.
source: Furthermore, the majority (23 out of 33) of the genes that were downregulated in response to cold belonged to the cluster 1 of genes whose expression negatively correlates with dormancy levels (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by data in Figure 2E and Figure 2—source data 5.

claim: At least a third of dormancy-specific MEGs are involved or potentially involved in regulating seed germination.
source: In summary, at least a third of dormancy-specific MEGs are involved or potentially involved in regulating seed germination.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of MEG functions.

claim: About half of dormancy-specific MEGs have their expression correlated negatively with seed dormancy levels.
source: Moreover, about half of dormancy-specific MEGs have their expression correlated negatively with seed dormancy levels.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on clustering analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Most dormancy-specific MEGs whose expression negatively correlates with dormancy levels have their expression downregulated by cold during seed development.
source: Among the latter, most have their expression downregulated by cold during seed development, which increases mature seed dormancy levels.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of cold response data in Figure 2E.

claim: CP1 encodes a predicted ortholog of radish DRCP26, which is involved in protein storage decay during the early phase of seed germination.
source: CP1 encodes a predicted ortholog of radish DRCP26, which is involved in protein storage decay during the early phase of seed germination (Tsuji et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Tsuji et al., 2013.

claim: CP1 expression is stringently regulated upon seed imbibition according to seed dormancy levels and cold temperatures during seed development.
source: We found that CP1 expression is stringently regulated upon seed imbibition according to seed dormancy levels and cold temperatures during seed development (Figure 3 and Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by expression data in Figure 3 and Figure 2—source data 5.

claim: In absence of dry after-ripening, CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds were unable to germinate up to five days after seed imbibition.
source: In absence of dry after-ripening, CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds were unable to germinate up to five days after seed imbibition.
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 3.

claim: CP1 mRNA could not be detected 36 hr after seed imbibition in non-after-ripened CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds.
source: CP1 mRNA could not be detected 36 hr after seed imbibition (Figure 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by qPCR data in Figure 3.

claim: After a short dry after-ripening period of 10 days, CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds did not germinate two days after imbibition but 60% of ColxCvi F1 seeds germinated five days thereafter while CvixCol F1 seeds did not.
source: After a short dry after-ripening period of 10 days, CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds did not germinate two days after imbibition but 60% of ColxCvi F1 seeds germinated five days thereafter while CvixCol F1 seeds did not.
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 3.

claim: CP1 mRNA expression could be detected 36 hr after imbibition in the endosperm of both CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds after short after-ripening, and it was preferentially maternal.
source: CP1 mRNA expression could be detected 36 hr after imbibition in the endosperm of both CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds, and Sanger sequencing confirmed that it was preferentially maternal (Figure 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by qPCR and Sanger sequencing data in Figure 3.

claim: CP1 maternal allele expression was higher in the endosperm of ColxCvi F1 seeds than in that of CvixCol F1 seeds after short after-ripening.
source: Furthermore, CP1 maternal allele expression was higher in the endosperm of ColxCvi F1 seeds than in that of CvixCol F1 seeds (Figure 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by qPCR data in Figure 3.

claim: After an intermediate after-ripening period of 20 days, CvixCol F1 seeds were still unable to germinate 2 and 5 days after imbibition, unlike ColxCvi F1 seeds whose populations germinated at about 40% and 100%, respectively.
source: We next considered an intermediate after-ripening time of 20 days, after which CvixCol F1 seeds were still unable to germinate 2 and 5 days after imbibition, unlike ColxCvi F1 seeds whose populations germinated at about 40% and 100%, respectively (Figure 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 3.

claim: In CvixCol F1 seeds after intermediate after-ripening, CP1 expression was higher than that in shortly after-ripened CvixCol F1 seeds but remained preferentially maternal and lower than that in ColxCvi F1 seeds.
source: In CvixCol F1 seeds, CP1 expression was higher than that in shortly after-ripened CvixCol F1 seeds (Figure 3). However, this expression remained preferentially maternal and lower than that in ColxCvi F1 seeds (Figure 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by qPCR and Sanger sequencing data in Figure 3.

claim: CP1 expression was no longer preferentially maternal in ColxCvi F1 seeds after intermediate after-ripening.
source: Furthermore, CP1 expression was no longer preferentially maternal in ColxCvi F1 seeds.
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by Sanger sequencing data in Figure 3.

claim: After a long after-ripening period of two months, CP1 expression was similarly high and biallelic in both CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds.
source: Finally, after a long after-ripening period of two months, CP1 expression was similarly high and biallelic in both CvixCol and ColxCvi F1 seeds (Figure 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by qPCR and Sanger sequencing data in Figure 3.

claim: CP1 preferential maternal allele expression is only found in dormant seeds.
source: These results confirm that CP1 preferential maternal allele expression is only found in dormant seeds (Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by expression data in Figure 2C and Figure 3.

claim: The expression levels of maternal CP1 alleles correlate negatively with dormancy levels.
source: Furthermore, the expression levels of maternal CP1 alleles correlate negatively with dormancy levels.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on expression analysis in Figure 3.

claim: As seeds lose dormancy, CP1 preferential maternal allele expression is lost and CP1 expression increases.
source: As seeds lose dormancy, CP1 preferential maternal allele expression is lost and CP1 expression increases.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on expression analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Cruciferins (CRUs) are highly abundant storage proteins present in endosperm and embryos that can be detected by coomassie dye staining in SDS-PAGE gels.
source: Cruciferins (CRUs) are highly abundant storage proteins present in endosperm and embryos that can be detected by coomassie dye staining in SDS-PAGE gels (Barthole et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Barthole et al., 2014.

claim: In the absence of dry after-ripening, WT CRU levels in the endosperm remained constant over time upon seed imbibition.
source: In the absence of dry after-ripening, WT CRU levels in the endosperm remained constant over time upon seed imbibition, consistent with the dormant state of the seeds (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot and coomassie staining data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In fully after-ripened seeds, endospermic CRUs levels rapidly decayed prior to germination.
source: By contrast, in fully after-ripened seeds, endospermic CRUs levels rapidly decayed prior to germination (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot and coomassie staining data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Following a short after-ripening period, endospermic decay of CRU proteins and germination took place upon imbibition, but both processes were delayed relative to fully after-ripened seeds.
source: Following a short after-ripening period that does not fully eliminate seed dormancy, endospermic decay of CRU proteins and germination took place upon imbibition, but both processes were delayed relative to fully after-ripened seeds (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot and coomassie staining data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Endospermic abundance of CRU proteins upon imbibition reflects seed dormancy levels.
source: Altogether, these results show that endospermic abundance of CRU proteins upon imbibition reflects seed dormancy levels.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on CRU protein analysis in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In fully after-ripened seeds, WT endosperm CRU levels rapidly decayed upon imbibition whereas in cp1 mutants, the decay of CRUs levels was delayed by at least 12 hr.
source: By contrast, in fully after-ripened seeds, WT endosperm CRU levels rapidly decayed upon imbibition whereas in cp1 mutants, the decay of CRUs levels was delayed by at least 12 hr (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot and coomassie staining data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The delay in CRU decay in cp1 mutants was not due to slower cp1 mutant germination as both testa rupture and endosperm rupture events proceeded at the same pace in WT and cp1 seeds.
source: This delay was not due to slower cp1 mutant germination as both testa rupture and endosperm rupture events proceeded at the same pace in WT and cp1 seeds, indicating that CP1 is not required to regulate germination sensu stricto (Weitbrecht et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and citation to Weitbrecht et al., 2011.

claim: CP1 is not required to regulate germination sensu stricto.
source: This delay was not due to slower cp1 mutant germination as both testa rupture and endosperm rupture events proceeded at the same pace in WT and cp1 seeds, indicating that CP1 is not required to regulate germination sensu stricto (Weitbrecht et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and citation to Weitbrecht et al., 2011.

claim: In shortly after-ripened seeds, CRU protein decay was delayed in cp1 mutant seeds relative to WT seeds even though cp1 and WT seed germination proceeded at the same pace.
source: Similarly, in shortly after-ripened seeds, CRU protein decay was delayed in cp1 mutant seeds relative to WT seeds even though cp1 and WT seed germination proceeded at the same pace (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot, coomassie staining, and germination data in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: During the early stages of germination, no differences in the accumulation of CRUs proteins could be detected between WT and cp1 embryos.
source: During the early stages of germination examined above, no differences in the accumulation of CRUs proteins could be detected between WT and cp1 embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot and coomassie staining data in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: CP1 is necessary to promote the decay of endosperm CRU proteins prior to the germination of shortly and fully after-ripened seeds.
source: Taken together, these data show that CP1 is necessary to promote the decay of endosperm CRU proteins prior to the germination of shortly and fully after-ripened seeds.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of cp1 mutants in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the absence of dry after-ripening or in fully after-ripened seeds, CRU protein levels were similar between WTxcp1 and cp1xWT F1 endosperm 36 hr after seed imbibition.
source: Consistent with this prediction, in the absence of dry after-ripening or in fully after-ripened seeds, CRU protein levels were similar between WTxcp1 and cp1xWT F1 endosperm 36 hr after seed imbibition (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot and coomassie staining data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In shortly after-ripened WTxcp1 and cp1xWT F1 seeds, CRU protein levels were higher in the cp1xWT F1 endosperm than in the WTxcp1 F1 endosperm 36 hr after imbibition.
source: By contrast, in shortly after-ripened WTxcp1 and cp1xWT F1 seeds, CRU protein levels were higher in the cp1xWT F1 endosperm than in the WTxcp1 F1 endosperm 36 hr after imbibition (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot and coomassie staining data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The cp1 mutant maternal allele imposes a delay in CRU decay only in intermediately dormant seeds in which CP1 preferential maternal allele expression could be detected in F1 seeds.
source: Therefore, the cp1 mutant maternal allele imposes a delay in CRU decay only in intermediately dormant seeds in which CP1 preferential maternal allele expression could be detected in F1 seeds (Figure 3).
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of reciprocal crosses in Figure 4B and expression data in Figure 3.

claim: Among seeds produced in the same cp1/CP1 silique, the decay of CRUs was delayed in cp1/cp1/CP1 endosperms relative to CP1/CP1/CP1 endosperms 36 hr after seed imbibition.
source: Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B show that among seeds produced in the same cp1/CP1 silique, the decay of CRUs was delayed in cp1/cp1/CP1 endosperms relative to CP1/CP1/CP1 endosperms 36 hr after seed imbibition.
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by western blot and coomassie staining data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The maternally imposed delay in the decay of CRU proteins results, at least in part, from cp1 mutant alleles present in the maternal gamete cells rather than in maternal sporophyte cells.
source: These results therefore show that the maternally imposed delay in the decay of CRU proteins results, at least in part, from cp1 mutant alleles present in the maternal gamete cells rather than in maternal sporophyte cells.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of heterozygous mother crosses in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ALN gene encodes allantoin amidohydrolase (allantoinase).
source: The ALN gene encodes allantoin amidohydrolase (allantoinase).
evidence: Directly stated in text.

claim: Allantoinase participates in the plant purine catabolism pathway by converting allantoin to allantoate, which is subsequently used for nitrogen remobilization.
source: Allantoinase participates in the plant purine catabolism pathway by converting allantoin to allantoate, which is subsequently used for nitrogen remobilization.
evidence: Directly stated in text.

claim: Increased allantoin levels in response to drought stress protects the plant by enhancing ABA synthesis.
source: In this context, Watanabe et al. showed that increased allantoin levels in response to drought stress protects the plant by enhancing ABA synthesis (Watanabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Watanabe et al., 2014.

claim: aln seedlings accumulate high ABA levels.
source: Indeed, Watanabe et al. showed that aln seedlings accumulate high ABA levels (Watanabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Watanabe et al., 2014.

claim: aln mutant seeds displayed high dormancy relative to WT seeds.
source: Indeed, we found that aln mutant seeds displayed high dormancy relative to WT seeds (Figure 5A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 5A.

claim: ALN is a negative regulator of seed dormancy.
source: Thus, ALN is a negative regulator of seed dormancy.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of aln mutant phenotype in Figure 5A.

claim: Implementation of seed dormancy in aln mutants required the presence of the endosperm.
source: As expected, implementation of seed dormancy in aln mutants required the presence of the endosperm (Figure 5A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by embryo dissection data in Figure 5A.

claim: After a short after-ripening period of three days, the germination percentage of alnxWT F1 seeds was low and comparable to that of aln mutants.
source: After a short after-ripening period of three days, the germination percentage of alnxWT F1 seeds was low and comparable to that of aln mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 5B.

claim: The germination percentage of WTxaln F1 seeds after short after-ripening was markedly higher and similar to that of WT seeds.
source: By contrast, the germination percentage of WTxaln F1 seeds was markedly higher and similar to that of WT seeds (Figure 5B).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 5B.

claim: The germination differences between alnxWT and WTxaln F1 seeds were no longer observed when the after-ripening time was prolonged to 14 days.
source: The germination differences between alnxWT and WTxaln F1 seeds were no longer observed when the after-ripening time was prolonged to 14 days whereas aln mutant seed germination remained significantly lower than that of WT (Figure 5B).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 5B.

claim: Preferential maternal allele expression of ALN in ColxCvi F1 seeds was detected in seeds after-ripened for three days but no longer detected after 14 days of after-ripening.
source: Consistent with our results with CP1, preferential maternal allele expression of ALN in ColxCvi F1 seeds was detected in seeds after-ripened for three days but no longer detected after 14 days of after-ripening (Figure 5C).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by Sanger sequencing data in Figure 5C.

claim: Seeds bearing aln/aln/ALN endosperm were significantly more dormant than those bearing ALN/ALN/ALN endosperm.
source: Although the differences in germination percentage were not as pronounced as those found with alnxWT and WTxaln F1 seeds, seeds bearing aln/aln/ALN endosperm were significantly more dormant than those bearing ALN/ALN/ALN endosperm.
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by germination data in Figure 5B.

claim: ALN negatively regulates dormancy at least in part by maternal gametophytic alleles.
source: These results therefore strongly indicate that ALN negatively regulates dormancy at least in part by maternal gametophytic alleles.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of heterozygous mother crosses in Figure 5B.

claim: Maternal dormancy inheritance involves the preferential maternal allele expression of regulators of seed dormancy upon seed imbibition.
source: Together, these observations suggest a model in which maternal dormancy inheritance involves the preferential maternal allele expression of regulators of seed dormancy upon seed imbibition.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of CP1 and ALN.

claim: Dormancy levels in hybrid seeds reflect the maternal genotype, reflected in the maternal expression levels or product activities of genes regulating dormancy.
source: Therefore, dormancy levels in hybrid seeds reflect the maternal genotype, reflected in the maternal expression levels or product activities of genes regulating dormancy (Figure 6).
evidence: Directly stated in text and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: CP1 maternal allelic mRNA accumulation increased over time after imbibition, indicating de novo and dormancy-specific maternal allele transcription.
source: Indeed, we found that CP1 maternal allelic mRNA accumulation increased over time after imbibition, indicating de novo and dormancy-specific maternal allele transcription (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by expression data in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: The MEGs and PEGs identified in non-dormant seeds probably involve maternal allelic transcription upon seed imbibition as they were not detected in dormant seeds.
source: Furthermore, the MEGs and PEGs identified in non-dormant seeds probably involve maternal allelic transcription upon seed imbibition as they were not detected in dormant seeds.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on comparison of imprinted genes in dormant vs non-dormant seeds.

claim: A dedicated parental-specific allele transcription program operates upon mature seed imbibition.
source: These observations support the notion of a dedicated parental-specific allele transcription program operating upon mature seed imbibition.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of imprinted gene expression dynamics.

claim: The majority of dormancy-specific MEGs whose expression correlates with dormancy levels also have their expression further regulated by cold during seed development.
source: Interestingly, the majority of dormancy-specific MEGs whose expression correlates with dormancy levels also have their expression further regulated by cold during seed development.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of cold response data in Figure 2E.

claim: Imprinted gene expression levels upon imbibition are adapted to the environmental cues perceived by the mother plant or by the developing seed tissues or both.
source: This suggests that imprinted gene expression levels upon imbibition are further adapted to the environmental cues perceived by the mother plant or by the developing seed tissues or both.
evidence: Directly stated in text based on analysis of cold response of imprinted genes.

claim: The number of PEGs identified in dormant seeds is markedly lower than that reported previously during early embryogenesis.
source: Consistent with this speculation, the number of PEGs identified in dormant seeds is markedly lower than that reported previously during early embryogenesis (Figure 2) (Pignatta et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by comparison in Figure 2B and citation to Pignatta et al., 2014.

claim: In Arabidopsis, the endosperm is essential to repress the germination of dormant seeds.
source: In Arabidopsis, the endosperm is essential to repress the germination of dormant seeds.
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Removing the testa and endosperm upon dormant seed imbibition triggers growth and greening of the embryo.
source: Indeed, removing the testa and endosperm upon dormant seed imbibition triggers growth and greening of the embryo (Bethke et al., 2007; Lee and Lopez-Molina, 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citations to Bethke et al., 2007 and Lee and Lopez-Molina, 2013.

claim: Removing the testa while leaving the endosperm layer surrounding the embryo does not trigger embryonic growth.
source: Furthermore, removing the testa while leaving the endosperm layer surrounding the embryo does not trigger embryonic growth (Bethke et al., 2007).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Bethke et al., 2007.

claim: The endosperm of dormant seeds is able to block embryonic growth by continuously synthesizing and releasing ABA towards the embryo.
source: A 'seed coat bedding assay', monitoring the growth of dissected embryos cultured on a layer of dissected endosperms with the testa still attached, showed that the endosperm of dormant seeds is able to block embryonic growth by continuously synthesizing and releasing ABA towards the embryo (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claim: In fully after-ripened seeds, the endosperm ceases to release sufficient ABA upon imbibition, thus allowing germination to take place.
source: In fully after-ripened seeds, the endosperm ceases to release sufficient ABA upon imbibition, thus allowing germination to take place (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claim: Mature seed dormancy is a vital plant trait that prevents germination out of season.
source: Mature seed dormancy is a vital plant trait that prevents germination out of season.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Programs of imprinted gene expression are adapted according to the dormancy status of the seed.
source: Remarkably, programs of imprinted gene expression are adapted according to the dormancy status of the seed.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract.

claim: Imprinted genes play a role in regulating germination processes.
source: We provide direct evidence that imprinted genes play a role in regulating germination processes and that preferential maternal allelic expression can implement maternal inheritance of seed dormancy levels.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract.

claim: Preferential maternal allelic expression can implement maternal inheritance of seed dormancy levels.
source: We provide direct evidence that imprinted genes play a role in regulating germination processes and that preferential maternal allelic expression can implement maternal inheritance of seed dormancy levels.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract.

claim: Arabidopsis mature seeds consist of a desiccated and highly resistant embryo surrounded by a single cell layer of endosperm and an external layer, the testa, consisting of dead integumentary maternal tissues.
source: Arabidopsis mature seeds consist of a desiccated and highly resistant embryo surrounded by a single cell layer of endosperm and an external layer, the testa, consisting of dead integumentary maternal tissues.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: The endosperm is triploid, bearing two maternal genomes and one paternal genome.
source: The endosperm is triploid, bearing two maternal genomes and one paternal genome, whereas the zygote is diploid, bearing one maternal and one paternal genome.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: The zygote is diploid, bearing one maternal and one paternal genome.
source: The endosperm is triploid, bearing two maternal genomes and one paternal genome, whereas the zygote is diploid, bearing one maternal and one paternal genome.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Primary seed dormancy is a property of freshly produced seeds whereby seed germination does not occur even under otherwise favorable germination conditions.
source: Primary seed dormancy, hereafter referred to as 'dormancy', is a property of freshly produced seeds whereby seed germination does not occur even under otherwise favorable germination conditions (Chahtane et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Chahtane et al., 2016.

claim: As they age, dry seeds lose dormancy, a process known as dry after-ripening.
source: As they age, dry seeds lose dormancy, a process known as dry after-ripening, i.e. they acquire the capacity to germinate under favorable germination conditions.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Final seed dormancy levels are strongly influenced by the climatic conditions experienced by the mother plant.
source: Final seed dormancy levels are strongly influenced by the climatic conditions experienced by the mother plant.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Cold temperatures lead to higher final dormancy levels in Arabidopsis mature seeds.
source: In particular, cold temperatures lead to higher final dormancy levels in Arabidopsis mature seeds (Kendall et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Kendall et al., 2011.

claim: The response of seed dormancy to cold temperatures is maternally controlled, and involves the genes FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) and FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT).
source: Interestingly, this response is maternally controlled, and involves the genes FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) and FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) (Chiang et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Chiang et al., 2009 and Chen et al., 2014.

claim: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a growth-repressive hormone that is essential to repress the germination of dormant seeds.
source: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a growth-repressive hormone that is essential to repress the germination of dormant seeds (Debeaujon and Koornneef, 2000; Ali-Rachedi et al., 2004).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Debeaujon and Koornneef, 2000 and Ali-Rachedi et al., 2004.

claim: Upon imbibition, ABA stimulates the expression of LATE EMBRYONIC ABUNDANT (LEA) genes, whose products promote osmotolerance.
source: Furthermore, upon imbibition, ABA stimulates the expression of LATE EMBRYONIC ABUNDANT (LEA) genes, whose products promote osmotolerance, and inhibits embryonic lipid catabolism (Lopez-Molina and Chua, 2000; Lopez-Molina et al., 2002; Penfield et al., 2006; Dekkers et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: ABA inhibits embryonic lipid catabolism upon seed imbibition.
source: Furthermore, upon imbibition, ABA stimulates the expression of LATE EMBRYONIC ABUNDANT (LEA) genes, whose products promote osmotolerance, and inhibits embryonic lipid catabolism (Lopez-Molina and Chua, 2000; Lopez-Molina et al., 2002; Penfield et al., 2006; Dekkers et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Genomic imprinting was found and studied in the endosperm during seed development in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis, genomic imprinting was found and studied in the endosperm during seed development (Gehring, 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Gehring, 2013.

claim: The occurrence and biological role of endospermic imprinting in Arabidopsis mature seeds has not been investigated previously.
source: The occurrence and biological role of endospermic imprinting in Arabidopsis mature seeds has not been investigated previously.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.
